problem: "happens here" is vague and "political society" shifts "society ... politically considered".
replacement: As soon as the multitude begins to take an interest in the labors of the mind, it finds that excelling in some of them is a powerful way to gain fame, power, or wealth. The restless ambition that equality produces at once takes this direction, as it does every other. The number of people who cultivate science, letters, and the arts becomes immense. The intellectual world springs into prodigious activity. Everyone tries to open a path there for himself and to draw the eyes of the public after him. Something similar occurs in the intellectual world to what happens in American society politically. What is done is often imperfect, but the attempts are countless. And although the results of individual effort are usually very small, the total is always very large.

problem: Bare "interest" rendered "self-interest" (twice), colliding with the fixed term for interest rightly understood.
replacement: Most of the men who make up these nations are extremely eager in the pursuit of actual, physical gratification. Since they are always dissatisfied with the position they hold and always free to leave it, they think of nothing but the means of changing their fortune or increasing it. To minds so disposed, every new method that leads by a shorter road to wealth, every machine that spares labor, every instrument that lowers the cost of production, and every discovery that makes pleasures easier or increases them seems the grandest effort of the human intellect. It is chiefly from these motives that a democratic people takes up scientific pursuits, understands them, and respects them. In aristocratic ages, science is called upon above all to provide gratification to the mind. In democracies, it is called upon to provide it to the body. You may be sure that the more democratic, educated, and free a nation is, the greater will be the number of these promoters of scientific genius who act out of interest, and the more discoveries that can be applied at once to productive industry will bring gain, fame, and even power to their authors. For in democracies the working class takes part in public affairs, and public honors, as well as financial rewards, may be given to those who deserve them. In a community organized in this way, it is easy to see that the human mind may be led, without noticing, to neglect theory, and that it is driven, on the contrary, with unparalleled vehemence toward the applications of science, or at least toward that portion of theoretical science which is necessary to those who make such applications. In vain will some innate inclination raise the mind toward the loftier spheres of the intellect: interest draws it down to the middle zone. There it can develop all its energy and restless activity, and there it can produce all its wonders. These very Americans, who have not discovered a single one of the general laws of mechanics, have introduced into navigation an engine that is changing the face of the world.

problem: "arrogant" softened to "proud"; the conditional "If" turned into an imperative "Suppose".
replacement: All I mean to say is this: permanent inequality of conditions leads men to confine themselves to the arrogant and sterile search for abstract truths, while the social condition and the institutions of democracy prepare them to seek the immediate, useful, practical results of the sciences. This tendency is natural and inevitable. It is worth knowing about, and it may be necessary to point it out. If those who are called upon to guide the nations of our time clearly saw from afar these new tendencies, which will soon be irresistible, they would understand that men living in democratic ages, possessing education and freedom, cannot fail to improve the industrial part of science, and that from now on all the efforts of the constituted authorities ought to be directed to supporting the highest branches of learning and to fostering the nobler passion for science itself. In the present age the human mind must be forced into theoretical studies. It runs of its own accord to practical applications, and instead of perpetually sending it back to the minute examination of secondary effects, it is good sometimes to turn it away from them, in order to raise it to the contemplation of primary causes. Because the civilization of ancient Rome perished as a result of the invasion of the barbarians, we are perhaps too ready to think that civilization cannot perish in any other way. If the light by which we are guided is ever extinguished, it will dwindle by degrees and die out of itself. By sticking closely to mere applications, people would lose sight of principles. When the principles were wholly forgotten, the methods derived from them would be badly pursued. New methods could no longer be invented, and men would go on applying, without intelligence and without art, scientific processes that were no longer understood.

problem: "manners" used where Tocqueville means customs (mores); style note requires "customs".
replacement: Three hundred years ago, when Europeans first reached China, they found that nearly all the arts had attained a certain degree of perfection there. They were surprised that a people who had come so far had never gone further. Later they found some traces of the higher branches of science, which had been lost. The nation was wrapped up in productive industry. Most of its scientific processes had been kept, but science itself no longer existed. That explained the strangely motionless state in which they found the Chinese mind. The Chinese, following in their forefathers’ footsteps, had forgotten the reasons that had guided those forefathers. They still used the formula without asking what it meant. They kept the instrument, but they had lost the art of altering or renewing it. The Chinese, then, had lost the power of change, and improvement was impossible for them. At all times and in all things they had to imitate their predecessors, for fear that by straying for a moment from the path laid down for them they would wander into total darkness. The source of human knowledge was almost dry. The stream still flowed, but it could neither swell its waters nor change its course. Even so, China had lasted in peace for centuries. The invaders who had conquered the country had taken on the customs of its inhabitants, and order prevailed. A kind of physical prosperity was visible everywhere. Revolutions were rare, and war was, so to speak, unknown.
